players.product: vacuum gauges, residual gas analyzers and in-situ process-control sensors

quarterly_data.signal: CEO Oliver Wyrsch: record Q2 2026 sales of $198 million, up 18% year on year, with Semiconductor & Vacuum Coating up 31% year on year (13% sequentially), General Vacuum up 11% (-3% sequentially, a timing effect with strong orders), RAC / Auto up 9% (13% sequentially) and Security & Energy down 31% year on year but up 55% on Q1, with strong Q2 orders, mainly from large US government programs. CFO Dimitrij Lisak: by region Asia-Pacific grew 32.5%, Europe 18.9%, Americas 18.7% and China 5.6% (a timing effect, with China orders nearly the highest); operating expenses rose 7.1% with R&D down 2.1% (around 7% of sales) and SG&A up 10.8%, and net income rose 76.4% to a 16.3% margin.
quarterly_data.figure: Q2 2026 sales $198 million, +18% year on year

quarterly_data.signal: CEO Oliver Wyrsch: semiconductor orders are 'not a normal ramp. This is the steepest we've ever seen', driven by the data-center build-out and the leading-edge logic and high-bandwidth memory tied to it, now spreading to communication, automotive, IoT, sensors, MEMS and power chips; logic and memory are about equally strong drivers, with HBM 'a bit more on fire' and memory a tad more exciting. He sees no double ordering or inventory building, notes market-share gains and new applications, and says order timelines are getting a bit longer while some expansion projects move out because other suppliers have delays, not demand; 'We are nowhere the bottleneck.' The raised guidance is 'a bit on the cautious side', and if more growth shows in Q3 there is a very high likelihood the guidance moves up materially again; Q3 may not show its usual seasonal weakness this year.

CEO Oliver Wyrsch: INFICON is now building the company out for over $1 billion of sales to deliver on the coming two years' projections; expansion projects are being implemented, with clean rooms taking one year+ with building expansions, tools six to nine months and staffing a couple of months, and many temps hired. CFO Dimitrij Lisak: full-year capex is raised from $30 million to roughly $35 million (Q2: $8.7 million), around 60% above prior-year capex. CEO: INFICON will spend R&D at 8%+ of sales in future; CFO: year-to-date R&D costs grow around 4%.
quarterly_data.figure: capacity being built for over $1 billion of sales; 2026 capex roughly $35 million

quarterly_data.signal: CEO Oliver Wyrsch: supply has so far kept up with only smaller hiccups: a choke hold around magnets has affected INFICON two times, there were concerns around PCBs, where it stocked up for buffer, and supplies of housing cables bottlenecked because data-center build-outs ate into the suppliers' capacity, with solutions found each time; bigger bottlenecks may come as the ramp continues. Lead times run from weeks for small sensors to two to three months for the largest systems, a little longer than usual.
quarterly_data.figure: lead times two to three months for the largest systems

quarterly_data.signal: CEO Oliver Wyrsch: INFICON has 80%+ global market share in mass spectrometry, with MKS probably the next largest; Atonarp, acquired by VAT, is a very small competitor concentrated on Japan. About 50% of semiconductor business is with OEM tool makers and the other half with chipmakers; OEM products carry 40s-50s% margins, chipmaker products 50%-60% and software the 80s%, so mix swings the gross margin. China sales are all direct, INFICON has manufactured there for over 25 years, and the CEO sees Chinese policy favouring fewer, stronger global players as a positive turn.

CEO Oliver Wyrsch: INFICON launched Arnova, a leak detection system that works with air and argon instead of increasingly expensive or scarce hydrogen, which he expects to be a breakthrough product. In RAC / Auto, automotive has not regained momentum while storage batteries (partly data-center driven) and HVAC (with a data-center driver) are growing; in General Vacuum, big science, space, robotics and life science are the more dynamic sub-markets while solar stays soft; rising defense budgets should drive Security & Energy further, though procurement is slow.
